title: My family
goal: Name family members, use possessives — including *ons* and *onze*, which follow the noun's group — and ask about age.
bekal: use *mijn, je, zijn, haar, ons/onze, hun* correctly
show possession with *van*: *de fiets van mijn broer*
wave: Review **Unit 3**: point at ten things around you, name each one with *de* or *het*, then make it plural.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Foto's op de telefoon
dialogs.intro: Sanne shows Budi photos of her family.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Wie is die man met de baard?
lines.id: Who's that man with the beard?
lines.literal: who is that man with the beard?

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Dat is mijn vader. Hij heet Kees.
lines.id: That's my father. His name is Kees.
lines.literal: that is my father. he is-called Kees.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: And the woman next to him?

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Mijn moeder, Anke. En dat zijn mijn twee broers.
lines.id: My mother, Anke. And those are my two brothers.
lines.literal: my mother, Anke. and that are my two brothers.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Tom is negentien en Daan is veertien. Ik ben de oudste.
lines.id: Tom is nineteen and Daan is fourteen. I'm the oldest.
lines.literal: Tom is nineteen and Daan is fourteen. I am the oldest.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Do you have a sister too?

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Nee. Maar mijn broer heeft een vriendin — die daar.
lines.id: No. But my brother has a girlfriend — that one there.
lines.literal: no. but my brother has a girlfriend — that-one there.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Ja, in haar huis in Haarlem. Ons huis is te klein.
lines.id: Yes, in her house in Haarlem. Our house is too small.
lines.literal: yes, in her house in Haarlem. our house is too small.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: En jullie hond? Is dat ook familie?
lines.id: And your dog? Is he family too?
lines.literal: and you-all's dog? is that also family?

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Onze hond is de baas van het huis.
lines.id: Our dog is the boss of the house.
lines.literal: our dog is the boss of the house.

notes: **Ons huis** but **onze hond** — this is the only Dutch possessive that changes shape. *Ons* for het-woorden, *onze* for de-woorden and for all plurals. The rest (*mijn, je, zijn, haar, jullie, hun*) never change at all.
**Wie is die man?** — *wie* = who, *wat* = what, *welke* = which. Watch out: *wie* looks like English *we* but means **who** — and is pronounced "vee".
**Naast hem** — after a preposition the object form is used: *hem* (him), *haar* (her), *mij/me* (me), *jou/je* (you), *ons* (us), *hen/hun* (them). Just like English "next to him", not "next to he".
**Hoe oud zijn ze?** Literally "how old are they?". Age is expressed with *zijn*, just as in English (*I am 25*) — not with *hebben* as in French or Spanish.
**De oudste** = the oldest. The degrees: *oud → ouder → oudst* (old → older → oldest). Comparison is covered fully in Unit 15.

**Een vriendin** means girlfriend **and** female friend — only the possessive tells them apart. *Mijn vriendin* usually means girlfriend; *een vriendin van mij* means a friend. The same goes for *vriend*.
**De baas van het huis** — possession is shown with *van* (of), not with an ending. This is by far the most common form in everyday Dutch.

grammars.title: Possessives
body: Eight possessives, and only one of them has two faces.
after: *Jouw* and *je* mean the same: *jouw* when you want emphasis (*Is dat jouw fiets of die van mij?*), *je* the rest of the time. The same goes for *m'n* and *z'n* in casual speech.
⚠️ *Zijn* means "his" **and** the verb "are". Its place in the sentence decides: *Zijn boek* (his book) versus *De boeken zijn nieuw* (the books are new).
⚠️ *Uw* (your, polite) is often confused with *u* (you, polite). *Hoe is uw naam?* is right; *Hoe is u naam?* is wrong.

grammars.title: Showing possession with van
body: Dutch has two ways, and the first is used far more than the second.

after: For things and ordinary nouns the *-s* form is **not** used: *het dak van het huis* (the roof of the house), never *het huis's dak*. Unlike English, Dutch has no general *'s*.
The question: *Van wie is deze tas?* ("Whose bag is this?") The answer: *Die is van mij.*

blocks.text: Many of these will feel familiar: *vader* and *moeder* are cousins of *father* and *mother*, *broer* of *brother*, *zoon* of *son*, *dochter* of *daughter*. *Opa* and *oma* are the everyday words — *grootvader* and *grootmoeder* sound like a history book.

blocks.title: Two words to handle with care
items: *De neef* means **male cousin** and **nephew**; *de nicht* the same for women. Dutch doesn't tell them apart — to be clear, people say *de zoon van mijn zus*.
*De man* means man **and** husband; *de vrouw* means woman **and** wife. The possessive makes the difference: *mijn man* = my husband.
Step-family takes the prefix *stief-*: *de stiefvader*. In-laws take *schoon-*: *de schoonouders*, *de zwager* (brother-in-law), *de schoonzus*.

blocks.text: *Jarig zijn* means "to be having your birthday" — a single adjective for something English needs a whole phrase for. And one Dutch custom that surprises newcomers: at a birthday party, **guests congratulate the whole family**, not just the birthday person — *gefeliciteerd met je zus!*
Notice too that Dutch numbers are read backwards: *vijfentwintig* = "five-and-twenty" = 25 — like the old English "four-and-twenty blackbirds". The system is taken apart completely in the next unit.

items: I have two brothers and a sister.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: ons — onze — onze — onze — ons — onze
Dit is mijn familie. — Hoe oud ben je? — Ik ben vijfentwintig jaar oud. — Ik heb twee broers en een zus. — Wie is die vrouw? — Van wie is deze fiets?
